newsitem.title: CANADA: Arakis sees drilling over 20 wells in '97.
newsitem.headline: Arakis sees drilling over 20 wells in '97.

text.p: Arakis Energy Corp, which last week announced a long-awaited joint venture to develop its oil concession in Sudan, expects the partners to drill over 20 wells on the 12.2 million acre concession in 1997, Arakis chief executive John McLeod said on Monday.
"A 20-plus well program is what we'll be looking at -- a combination of exploration, delineation and development," McLeod said in an interview.

Arakis had set a budget for 12 wells before the announcement of the joint venture deal, which would see US$1 billion being spent over the next few years on drilling and construction of a 950-mile oil pipeline.
But drilling was expected to be accelerated with the doubling to four of rigs working the Heglig and Unity fields.

Partners in the joint venture include Arakis with 25 percent, China National Petroleum Corp with 40 percent, Malaysia state-owned oil company Petronas Caligali with 30 percent and the Sudan government with five percent.
The consortium aims to begin shipping 150,000 barrels per day of oil to the Red Sea from southern Sudan by 1999.
Estimates for the cost of the pipeline, for which construction is expected to go to international bidders, are in the range of US$600 million.
Arakis shares on Monday were trading down 9/16 at 5 with 4.9 million shares changing hands in Nasdaq trade.

McLeod said a part of the deal which had not yet been emphasized was that the commitment period on its concession was extended by the Sudanese government by two years to November 1998. "Now, we've got another two dry seasons to complete a work program," he said.

Under the deal, Arakis will receive credit for nearly all of the US$140 million it has spent to date on exploration and development, plus credit for "appraised value-added," or improvements made to the properties, for a total of about US$200 million, McLeod said.

"As we go forward, we should not be spending any money until these (partners) cough up about US$600 million. "Half of that would get the upstream done and if there's the ability to put some financing against the pipeline it is possible we could get to cash flow without any additional cash required."
Some market watchers familiar with the Arakis saga said on Monday that the company negotiated a favorable deal, despite the absense of a hoped-for U.S. partner.

Kirk Dornbush, president of Atlanta-based Diem Investments, which holds Arakis stock in a hedge fund, said CNPC and Petronas were both highly regarded in world oil circles and were motivated to see the project to completion.

"If (a U.S. company) were involved, I think Arakis's role in the project would be diminished on an ongoing basis," Dornbush said. "Having CNPC and Petronas gives Arakis a more important role in the joint venture."

He said his calculations show that every 100 million barrels of proved and probable reserves is worth US$1 per share to the company. Arakis has said it was comfortable with current estimates of 600 million barrels, although analysts have said the total could be several times that.
When about 50 cents per share in cash and the deal's US$200 million of production and other operating credits were factored in, Arakis's net asset value would be about US$8.50 per share, he said.
However, the valuation makes nothing of Sudan's political risk, demonstrated Sunday by a shooting incident at an Arakis drilling location. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
